slides.title: The 3 Admin Surfaces — Why RBAC Always Needs Humans
slides.subtitle: Project Setup · Employee Setup · User Management

list.name: Project Setup
list.desc: Create / edit / archive projects. Define the project taxonomy YOUR client uses. AI doesn't know if your client groups by client-name, by domain, or by cost-center. You decide, then prompt.

list.name: Employee Setup
list.desc: Employee directory — the canonical 'who works here'. Includes employee number, name, email, active flag. Drives every Issue's assignee and reporter pickers.

list.name: User Management
list.desc: Login accounts mapped to Employees. Role assignment. Activate / deactivate. Reset password. AI doesn't know your org chart — YOU map it.

list.name: RBAC matrix
list.desc: The cross-product. Which role does what across these three surfaces. Reporters can't delete projects. Managers can. Admin can do everything including delete users (per FDD §17).

slides.memory_hook: 3 surfaces + RBAC = the org chart in code. AI can build the surfaces. You decide the RBAC.

slides.title: The Admin Prompt — One Prompt Per Surface
slides.subtitle: Same 8-component intent · RBAC clause is non-negotiable
bullets: Unlike Workflow (ONE long prompt), admin surfaces work best as 3 focused prompts — one per surface.
Why? Each surface has different RBAC, different validation, different list/detail UX. Splitting keeps each tight.
EVERY admin prompt must include: 'RBAC: which role can do what (matrix below). Server enforces on every endpoint. UI hides actions a role cannot perform.'
Example RBAC clause for Project Setup: 'Admin: full CRUD. Manager: full CRUD on their accessible projects. Reporter: read-only on their accessible projects. Server-side check at controller layer.'
Commit after EACH surface validates. 3 surfaces = 3 commits = 3 push events on Day 6.
slides.memory_hook: 3 surfaces · 3 prompts · 3 RBAC clauses · 3 commits. Tight, focused, auditable.

slides.title: Day 6 Afternoon — Reports
slides.subtitle: The first artifact your client's CEO will actually look at
slides.opening_hook: Dashboards are for users. Reports are for executives. The exec opens ONE Excel file from the email — make it land.
bullets: 8 reports in the Issue Tracker FDD — exec summary, by project, by reporter, by assignee, overdue aging, full register, weekly trend, priority matrix.
Every report has TWO outputs: Excel + PDF. Both must render. Both must look executive-grade.
Filters on every report: project, date range, status, type. Server applies them; results never leak across tenants.
Reports = the artifact your client's CEO opens. They tell the story your dashboard couldn't fit on one screen.

slides.title: The Reports Prompt — Excel + PDF in One Pass
slides.subtitle: References FDD §18 · uses exceljs + pdfkit · cached by query hash

hero_stat.label: × 2 formats (Excel + PDF) × 4 filters each = 64 report variations · generated from 1 reports module prompt

bullets: OUTCOME: Logged-in Admin/Manager runs a report → previews table → downloads Excel OR PDF.
STACK: NestJS reports module · Prisma aggregation queries · exceljs for .xlsx · pdfkit for .pdf · React Query for caching.
ACCEPTANCE: Each report < 3s for 10k issues. Excel opens cleanly in MS Excel + Google Sheets + LibreOffice. PDF prints landscape with vThink branding.
EDGE CASES: Empty result set → friendly 'no data' state, NOT a broken empty file. Large dataset → server streams response, no memory bloat.
RBAC: Reporters CANNOT access /reports (route guard + UI hide). Admins + Managers can. Tenant isolation enforced via Prisma where-clauses.

slides.title: Where Reports Break — And How to Catch It Pre-QA
slides.subtitle: 5 common AI report bugs · each one caught by manual spot-check

table.orch: ✅ Date columns formatted as dates, numbers as numbers, currency formatted
✅ Repeat header on each page, no orphan rows
✅ Prisma where-clause scopes by user.tenantId on every report query
✅ Reporter names, assignee names, project names — never UUIDs in exec reports
✅ Prisma raw SQL + indexes + LIMIT cap (e.g. 50k) with note in subtitle

slides.memory_hook: Open EVERY report in Excel + PDF before saying done. AI is great at structure, weak at finish.
slides.closing_thread: Reports shipped. Now the BIG handoff — to QA.

slides.title: Manual Validation — Open Every Report Yourself
slides.subtitle: 10 minutes · the cheapest QA you'll ever do
bullets: Run each of the 8 reports with default filters. Spot check the numbers against the dashboard. They should match.
Download each as Excel. Open in MS Excel. Open in Google Sheets. Open in LibreOffice. ALL THREE should render cleanly.
Download each as PDF. Open in Preview / Adobe. Print preview — landscape, branded, no orphan rows.
Try one report as a Reporter user — should get 403. Try one report with a 5-year date range — should not crash.
All green? git add . && git commit -m 'feat(reports): 8 reports validated end-to-end' && git push. Day 6 done.
slides.memory_hook: 10-minute report smoke test. Cheapest QA in the world. Catches 80% of report bugs before they hit a client.

slides.title: The Smoke Checklist — Your 15-Minute Daily Ritual
slides.subtitle: 9 cases. Every build. Pre-deploy. Sacred.

hero_stat.label: the daily smoke checklist · 9 cases · catches 80% of regressions before anyone deploys

bullets: AUTH-001 — Login (valid email + password → dashboard, JWT stored)
DASH-001 — Dashboard loads, 4 cards populated, no console errors
ISSA-001 + ISSA-007 — Issue list loads + detail opens with correct ID
ISNEW-001 — Create issue (happy path), defect number assigned, appears in list
CMT-002 — Post comment with current status (no transition record)
CMT-003 — Post comment with new status (transition fires, audit log records)
PWD-001 — Change password works, login with new password works
RBAC — Reporter visits /reports → redirected (route guard works)
RPT-006 — Full issue register opens, exports to Excel + PDF cleanly
slides.memory_hook: 9 cases. 15 minutes. EVERY build. If anything fails — STOP deploy, re-prompt, smoke again.
slides.closing_thread: Bugs WILL surface. How you handle them defines your reputation.

slides.title: The Real-Time Defect Loop
slides.subtitle: QA finds a bug · you re-prompt while they watch · validate together · commit
bullets: QA finds bug → reads the test ID + observed behaviour aloud (e.g. 'TRN-011, expected dialog, got inline form').
You open the file referenced in your re-prompt notes from Module 5. Compose surgical re-prompt.
AI generates fix in ~3 min. You hot-reload. QA re-runs the test case. Live. Together.
If green: git add → commit 'fix(workflow): TRN-011 reopen dialog' → push. ONE bug, ~10 min, closed.
If still red: you and QA debug together. Read the diff. Identify what AI mis-interpreted. Tighter re-prompt. Repeat.

slides.title: UAT With the Client — Collaboration, Not Gatekeeping
slides.subtitle: The client isn't validating your work · they're shaping the product
bullets: UAT happens with the CLIENT in the room (in person or screen-share). You drive. They watch + react.
Real client feedback in OrchestrAI engagements isn't 'this is broken' — it's 'this is right but I want it differently'.
Hot tip: when a client says 'can it do X?' and X is in scope — answer in the moment with a re-prompt. Show them in 5 min.
When X is out of scope — log it, propose phase 2. Don't say no. Don't say yes. Say 'great idea, here's how we sequence it.'
UAT sign-off = your client champions you internally. They tell THEIR boss 'this team delivered in 7 days what we've waited 7 months for.'
